abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p:
We strengthen a result of Bagaria and Magidor (Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 366 (2014), no. 4, 1857–1877) about the relationship between large cardinals and torsion classes of abelian groups, and prove that
(1)the Maximum Deconstructibility principle introduced in Cox (J. Pure Appl. Algebra 226 (2022), no. 5) requires large cardinals; it sits, implication‐wise, between Vopěnka's Principle and the existence of an ω1$\omega _1$‐strongly compact cardinal. (2)While deconstructibility of a class of modules always implies the precovering property by Saorín and Šťovíček (Adv. Math. 228 (2011), no. 2, 968–1007), the concepts are (consistently) nonequivalent, even for classes of abelian groups closed under extensions, homomorphic images, and colimits.

section.title: INTRODUCTION
section.p: Approximation theory of modules provides tools for studying general modules by choosing special classes of modules and finding approximations (precovers and preenvelopes), and minimal approximations (covers and envelopes), of the general modules by modules in the chosen classes.

A model case is the special class P0$\mathcal {P}_0$ of projective modules that yields projective precovers, and projective resolutions of modules. Similarly, the class F0$\mathcal {F}_0$ of flat modules yields flat covers, and minimal flat resolutions of modules, [5]. Dually, the class I0$\mathcal {I}_0$ of injective modules yields injective envelopes, and minimal injective coresolutions of modules.

In the case when minimal approximations exist, they provide invariants of modules, the model examples being Bass' invariants and dual Bass' invariants of modules over commutative Noetherian rings [11].

Approximation theory makes it possible to extend classic homological algebra to the setting of relative homological algebra [10]. Applications of the extended setting are numerous: in the theory of finitely generated modules over artin algebras [2], tilting theory of commutative Noetherian rings [14], and Gorenstein homological algebra [15], to name a few.

Classic structure theory of modules is based on decompositions into (possibly infinite) direct sums of indecomposable modules. This is a strong tool in the study of modules of finite length and injective modules over commutative Noetherian rings [1]. However, decomposability fails for many other classes of interest. In contrast, the weaker notion of deconstructibility (namely, decomposition into a transfinite extension of modules from a given set of modules) is almost omnipresent.

The key point is that deconstructible classes of modules always provide precovers, that is, each deconstructible class is precovering [18]. The opposite question is more subtle. 1 Question
Suppose C$\mathcal {C}$ is a class of modules that is precovering and closed under transfinite extensions. Is C$\mathcal {C}$ deconstructible?

In this paper, we use some results of Bagaria and Magidor from [3] to provide a negative answer to Question 1, at least in the absence of large cardinals:
Theorem
If there are no ω1$\omega _1$‐strongly compact cardinals, then there is a precovering class of abelian groups that is closed under transfinite extensions, homomorphic images, and colimits, but is not deconstructible.

In fact, the torsion class ⊥0Z:={A∈Ab:Hom(A,Z)=0}$$\begin{equation*} {}^{\perp _0} \mathbb {Z}:= \lbrace A \in {\bf Ab} \ : \ \text{Hom}(A,\mathbb {Z})=0 \rbrace \end{equation*}$$is always a covering class that is closed under transfinite extensions, homomorphic images, and colimits. In this respect we prove:
2 Theorem
⊥0Z${}^{\perp _0} \mathbb {Z}$ is deconstructible if and only if there is an ω1$\omega _1$‐strongly compact cardinal.

Theorem 2 strengthens a result of Bagaria and Magidor, who got the same equivalence with “deconstructible” weakened to “bounded” (we show in Lemma 11 that these concepts are equivalent, for any class of modules closed under transfinite extensions, homomorphic images, and colimits).

In [6], the first author proved that any deconstructible class is:
(a)closed under transfinite extensions (by definition), and (b)“eventually almost everywhere closed under quotients”. This is an extremely weak version of saying that if A⊂B$A \subset B$ are both in the class, then so is B/A$B/A$. In particular, it holds if the class is closed under homomorphic images.
He introduced the Maximum Deconstructiblity principle, which asserts that any class satisfying both (a) and (b) is deconstructible, and proved that
Vopěnka's Principle (VP) implies Maximum Deconstructibility.

Maximum Deconstructibility appeared very powerful, since [6] showed that it implied deconstructibility of many classes in Gorenstein homological algebra that (so far) are not known to be deconstructible in ZFC alone. But it was unclear whether Maximum Deconstructibility had any large cardinal strength at all. We again use the results of Bagaria and Magidor to show that it does:
Theorem
Maximum Deconstructibility implies the existence of an ω1$\omega _1$‐strongly compact cardinal.
So, Maximum Deconstructibility lies, implication‐wise, between VP and the existence of an ω1$\omega _1$‐strongly compact cardinal. The first author still conjectures that it is equivalent to VP.

Section 2 has preliminaries. Section 3 proves the approximation properties of torsion classes that are provable in ZFC alone. Section 4 discusses some results of Bagaria–Magidor [3]. Section 5 proves the main theorems mentioned above, and Section 6 includes some questions.

section.title: PRELIMINARIES
section.p:
Our notation and conventions follow Kanamori [16] (for set theory and large cardinals) and Göbel–Trlifaj [14] (for module theory). By ring we will mean a unital and not necessarily commutative ring. If R$R$ is a ring, the class of left R$R$‐modules will be denoted by R$R$‐Mod. We will say that M$M$ is a module rather than a left R$R$‐module whenever R$R$ is clear from the context. For a regular cardinal κ$\kappa$ and a module M$M$, the collection of all submodules N$N$ of M$M$ that are <κ${<}\kappa$‐generated will be denoted by [M]<κ$[M]^{<\kappa }$; if |R|<κ$|R|<\kappa$ and κ$\kappa$ is regular and uncountable, then “<κ${<}\kappa$‐generated” is equivalent to “of cardinality less than κ$\kappa$”. A cardinal κ$\kappa$ is strongly compact if every κ$\kappa$‐complete filter (on any set whatsoever) can be extended to a κ$\kappa$‐complete ultrafilter. Bagaria and Magidor considered a weakening of strong compactness:
3 Definition Bagaria and Magidor [3]
An uncountable cardinal κ$\kappa$ is called ω1$\omega _1$‐strongly compact if every κ$\kappa$‐complete filter extends to an ω1$\omega _1$‐complete ultrafilter.

Note that if κ$\kappa$ is ω1$\omega _1$‐strong compact then so is any cardinal λ⩾κ$\lambda \geqslant \kappa$. Unlike strongly compact cardinals, an ω1$\omega _1$‐strong compact cardinal may fail to be regular [3, section 6].

section.title: APPROXIMATION PROPERTIES AND TORSION CLASSES
section.p:
Given a class K$\mathcal {K}$ of R$R$‐modules, a K$\mathcal {K}$‐filtration is a ⊆$\subseteq$‐increasing and ⊆$\subseteq$‐continuous sequence ⟨Mξ∣ξ<η⟩$\langle M_\xi \mid \xi <\eta \rangle$ of modules such that M0=0$M_0=0$ and for all ξ<η$\xi <\eta$ such that ξ+1<η$\xi +1<\eta$, Mξ$M_\xi$ is a submodule of Mξ+1$M_{\xi +1}$ and Mξ+1/Mξ$M_{\xi +1}/M_\xi$ is isomorphic to a member of K$\mathcal {K}$. A module M$M$ is K$\mathcal {K}$‐filtered whenever there is a K$\mathcal {K}$‐filtration ⟨Mξ∣ξ<η⟩$\langle M_\xi \mid \xi <\eta \rangle$ whose union is M$M$. We shall denote the class of all K$\mathcal {K}$‐filtered modules by Filt(K)$\mathrm{Filt}(\mathcal {K})$. K$\mathcal {K}$ is closed under transfinite extensions whenever Filt(K)⊆K$\mathrm{Filt}(\mathcal {K})\subseteq \mathcal {K}$. Finally, K<κ$\mathcal {K}^{<\kappa }$ denotes the class of all <κ${<}\kappa$‐presented members of K$\mathcal {K}$.
4 Definition
Let K$\mathcal {K}$ be a class of modules and λ⩽κ$\lambda \leqslant \kappa$ be regular cardinals.
(1)K$\mathcal {K}$ is κ$\kappa$‐deconstructible whenever K=FiltK<κ$\mathcal {K} = \mathrm{Filt}\left({\mathcal {K}}^{<\kappa } \right)$; equivalently, K$\mathcal {K}$ is closed under transfinite extensions, and every M∈K$M\in \mathcal {K}$ admits a K<κ${\mathcal {K}}^{<\kappa }$‐filtration.†
This is the definition of deconstructibility in most newer references, such as [19], since it is the version that (by [18]) implies the precovering property. Some other sources (e.g., Cox [6], Göbel–Trlifaj [14]) only require that K⊆FiltK<κ$\mathcal {K} \subseteq \mathrm{Filt}\left({\mathcal {K}}^{<\kappa } \right)$ (i.e., with ⊆$\subseteq$ rather than equality). (2)K$\mathcal {K}$ is (κ,λ)$(\kappa,\lambda)$‐cofinal if K∩[M]<κ$\mathcal {K}\cap [M]^{<\kappa }$ is ⊆$\subseteq$‐cofinal in [M]<λ$[M]^{<\lambda }$ for every module M∈K$M\in \mathcal {K}$ (i.e., whenever every N∈[M]<λ$N\in [M]^{<\lambda }$ is contained in some <κ${<}\kappa$‐generated submodule of M$M$ that lies in K$\mathcal {K}$). (3)K$\mathcal {K}$ is bounded by κ$\kappa$ whenever M=∑K∩[M]<κ$M=\sum \left(\mathcal {K}\cap [M]^{<\kappa } \right)$ for all M∈K$M\in \mathcal {K}$ (i.e., if every x∈M$x \in M$ is contained in some <κ${<}\kappa$‐generated submodule of M$M$ that lies in K$\mathcal {K}$).‡
This property was introduced by Gardner in [13] and later investigated by Dugas in [9]. (4)K$\mathcal {K}$ is κ$\kappa$‐decomposable if every module in K$\mathcal {K}$ is a direct sum of <κ${<}\kappa$‐presented modules from K$\mathcal {K}$.
K$\mathcal {K}$ is said to be deconstructible provided it is κ$\kappa$‐deconstructible for a regular cardinal κ$\kappa$. The same convention is applied to the rest of above‐mentioned properties.

Clearly, any (κ,λ)$(\kappa,\lambda)$‐cofinal class is bounded by κ$\kappa$. In the forthcoming Lemma 11, we will argue that for certain classes K$\mathcal {K}$, “bounded by κ$\kappa$” and “(κ,κ)$(\kappa,\kappa)$‐cofinal” are equivalent concepts.

The following definitions are due to Enochs (generalizing earlier work of Auslander):
5 Definition
Let K$\mathcal {K}$ be a class of modules. We say that K$\mathcal {K}$ is:
(1)Precovering: if every module M$M$ posseses a K$\mathcal {K}$‐precover; namely, a morphism f:C→M$f\colon C\rightarrow M$ with C∈K$C\in \mathcal {K}$ such that Hom(D,f)$\mathrm{Hom}(D,f)$ is surjective for all D∈K;$D\in \mathcal {K};$ (2)Covering: If every module M$M$ posseses a K$\mathcal {K}$‐cover; namely, a K$\mathcal {K}$‐precover f:C→M$f\colon C\rightarrow M$ such that for each g∈End(C)$g\in \mathrm{End}(C)$ if fg=f$fg=f$ then g$g$ is an automorphism of C$C$.

Saorín and Šťovíček [18] proved that if a class K$\mathcal {K}$ (of, say, modules) is deconstructible, then it is precovering. In Section 5, we argue that there are nicely behaved covering classes which are yet, at least consistently, not deconstructible. The concrete example we have in mind is the torsion class of the abelian group Z$\mathbb {Z}$ in a context where the set‐theoretic universe does not have any ω1$\omega _1$‐strongly compact cardinals (see Definition 3).

Dickson [8] introduced the concept of torsion pairs, which are pairs (A,B)$(\mathcal {A},\mathcal {B})$ such that A=⊥0B:={X:Hom(X,B)=0for allB∈B}$$\begin{equation*} \mathcal {A} = {}^{\perp _0} \mathcal {B}:= \lbrace X \ : \ \text{Hom}(X,B)=0 \text{ for all } B \in \mathcal {B} \rbrace \end{equation*}$$and B=A⊥0:={Y:Hom(A,Y)=0for allA∈A}.$$\begin{equation*} \mathcal {B} = \mathcal {A}^{\perp _0}:= \lbrace Y \ : \ \text{Hom}(A,Y)=0 \text{ for all } A \in \mathcal {A} \rbrace . \end{equation*}$$A class of modules is called a torsion class if it is of the form ⊥0B${}^{\perp _0} \mathcal {B}$ for some class B$\mathcal {B}$; notice that in this situation, ⊥0B,⊥0B⊥0$$\begin{equation*} {\left({}^{\perp _0} \mathcal {B}, {\left({}^{\perp _0} \mathcal {B} \right)}^{\perp _0} \right)} \end{equation*}$$is easily seen to be a torsion pair (the torsion pair cogenerated by B$\mathcal {B}$). So, torsion classes are exactly those classes that are the left part of some torsion pair. Whenever X$\mathcal {X}$ is a singleton {X}$\lbrace X \rbrace$, the convention is to write ⊥0X${}^{\perp _0} X$ rather than ⊥0{X}${}^{\perp _0}\lbrace X\rbrace$.

By [8], torsion classes are exactly those classes that are closed under arbitrary direct sums, extensions, and homomorphic images [20, Proposition VI.2.1]. They have many other desirable features; we list the ones that are relevant for this paper.
6 Lemma
Torsion classes are:
(1)closed under homomorphic images, (2)closed under colimits, (3)closed under transfinite extensions, (4)covering classes.

(1) is immediate from the definition of torsion class, and (2) follows from closure under direct sums and homomorphic images. Closure under transfinite extensions follows easily from closure under extensions and colimits. Finally, given any module M$M$ and any torsion class T:=⊥0X$\mathcal {T}:={}^{\perp _0} \mathcal {X}$, the trace of T$\mathcal {T}$ in M$M$ is defined as r(M):=∑T∈T{imπ:π∈Hom(T,M)}.$$\begin{equation*} r(M):= \sum _{T \in \mathcal {T}} \lbrace \text{im} \ \pi \ : \ \pi \in \text{Hom}(T,M) \rbrace . \end{equation*}$$Then it is easily seen that r(M)∈T$r(M) \in \mathcal {T}$ and that the inclusion r(M)→M$r(M) \rightarrow M$ is a T$\mathcal {T}$‐cover of M$M$.

section.title: ON SOME RESULTS OF BAGARIA AND MAGIDOR
section.p:
In Bagaria–Magidor [3, section 5], a torsion class ⊥0X${}^{\perp _0} \mathcal {X}$ is called “κ$\kappa$‐generated” whenever every A∈⊥0X$A \in {}^{\perp _0} \mathcal {X}$ is a direct sum of subgroups in ⊥0X${}^{\perp _0} \mathcal {X}$, each of cardinality <κ${<}\kappa$; this is what is usually called κ$\kappa$‐decomposable (see Definition 4). The use of the word “direct” on [3, p. 1867] appears to be a misprint,†
The anonymous referee has suggested that the authors of [3] might have intended to say directed sum instead of direct sum. since the arguments there never use (or conclude) directness of the relevant sums. The arguments in [3, section 5], and the citation they provide for the concept (Dugas [9]), appear to use the weaker property that every group in the class is a sum of subgroups in the class of cardinality <κ${<}\kappa$. The latter condition is what we called bounded by κ$\kappa$ in Section 2 (this terminology was used by Gardner [13] and Dugas [9]). So, we shall use the bounded by κ$\kappa$ terminology to state the Bagaria–Magidor results. They proved the following.
7 Theorem [3, Theorem 5.1]
If κ$\kappa$ is a δ$\delta$‐strongly compact cardinal and X$X$ is an abelian group of cardinality less than δ$\delta$, then ⊥0X${}^{\perp _0} X$ is bounded by κ$\kappa$. In fact, they prove the stronger property of ⊥0X${}^{\perp _0} X$ being (κ,ω1)$(\kappa,\omega _1)$‐cofinal.‡
Recall that this stands for the following property: For each G∈⊥0Z$G\in {}^{\perp _0}\mathbb {Z}$, every countable subgroup H⩽G$H\leqslant G$ is included in a member of ⊥0Z∩[G]<κ${}^{\perp _0}\mathbb {Z}\cap [G]^{<\kappa }$ (see Definition 4).

mathStatement.title: Theorem
mathStatement.p: If ⊥0Z${}^{\perp _0} \mathbb {Z}$ is bounded in κ$\kappa$, then κ$\kappa$ is ω1$\omega _1$‐strongly compact.

mathStatement.title: Corollary
mathStatement.p: ⊥0Z${}^{\perp _0} \mathbb {Z}$ is bounded in κ$\kappa$ if and only if κ$\kappa$ is ω1$\omega _1$‐strongly compact.

section.p:
The following ZFC theorem (due to the third author) shows that, while ⊥0Z${}^{\perp _0} \mathbb {Z}$ can be bounded (by the Bagaria–Magidor results), it can never be decomposable:
10 Theorem
⊥0Z${}^{\perp _0} \mathbb {Z}$ is not decomposable.

mathStatement.title: Proof
mathStatement.p:
Suppose toward a contradiction that ⊥0Z${}^{\perp _0} \mathbb {Z}$ is κ$\kappa$‐decomposable, with κ$\kappa$ (without loss of generality) a regular uncountable cardinal. Fix any prime p$p$. Then all p$p$‐groups†
Abelian groups whose elements all have order a power of p$p$. are in ⊥0Z${}^{\perp _0} \mathbb {Z}$. So, in particular, the κ$\kappa$‐decomposability assumption of ⊥0Z${}^{\perp _0} \mathbb {Z}$ implies 1 Everyp-group is a direct sum of<κ-sized subgroups.$$\begin{equation} \text{Every } p \text{-group is a direct sum of } < \kappa \text{-sized subgroups.} \end{equation}$$

For a p$p$‐group G$G$, we can consider its p$p$‐length, which is the least ordinal σ$\sigma$ such that Gσ=Gσ+1$G_\sigma = G_{\sigma +1}$, where Gσ$G_\sigma$ is defined recursively by G0:=G$G_0:=G$, Gσ+1={pg:g∈Gσ}$G_{\sigma +1} = \lbrace p g \ : \ g \in G_\sigma \rbrace$, and Gσ=∩ξ<σGξ$G_\sigma = \bigcap _{\xi < \sigma } G_\xi$ for limit ordinals σ$\sigma$. By a construction of Walker [21] (see also Bazzoni–Šťovíček [4]), there exists a p$p$‐group, denoted Pκ+$P_{\kappa ^+}$, whose p$p$‐length is exactly κ++1$\kappa ^+ +1$.‡
The group is indexed by strictly decreasing finite sequences of ordinals κ+>β1>...>βk$\kappa ^+ > \beta _1 > . . . > \beta _k$, with relations p(κ+β1...βk+1)=κ+β1...βk$p(\kappa ^+\beta _1 . . . \beta _{k+1}) = \kappa ^+\beta _1 . . . \beta _k$ and p(κ+)=0$p(\kappa ^+) = 0$. By (1), Pκ+=⨁i∈IQi$$\begin{equation*} P_{\kappa ^+} = \bigoplus _{i \in I} Q_i \end{equation*}$$for some collection (Qi)i∈I$(Q_i)_{i \in I}$ of <κ$<\kappa$‐sized subgroups. Since subgroups of p$p$‐groups are also p$p$‐groups, each Qi$Q_i$ has a p$p$‐length, which is <κ$<\kappa$ because |Qi|<κ$|Q_i|<\kappa$. And it is easy to check that the p$p$‐length of a direct sum is at most the supremum of the p$p$‐lengths of the direct summands, so ⨁i∈IQi$\bigoplus _{i \in I} Q_i$ has p$p$‐length at most κ$\kappa$, contradicting that the p$p$‐length of Pκ+$P_{\kappa ^+}$ is κ++1$\kappa ^+ + 1$.□$\Box$

section.title: MAXIMUM DECONSTRUCTIBILITY, AND DECONSTRUCTIBILITY OF TORSION CLASSES, REQUIRE LARGE CARDINALS

mathStatement.title: Proof
mathStatement.p: The (a) ⇒$\Rightarrow$ (b) direction follows from the Hill Lemma (cf. Göbel–Trlifaj [14, Theorem 7.10]). The (b) ⇒$\Rightarrow$ (c) implication is immediate from the definitions.

Now suppose K$\mathcal {K}$ is closed under transfinite extensions and quotients. We prove (b) ⇒$\Rightarrow$ (a). Without losing any generality, we may assume that (the universe of) every module M∈K$M\in \mathcal {K}$ is a cardinal. Since K$\mathcal {K}$ is closed both under transfinite extensions and quotients, and |R|<κ$|R|<\kappa$, then by [6, Theorem 6.3] in order to prove κ$\kappa$‐deconstructibility of K$\mathcal {K}$ it suffices to show that if M∈K$M \in \mathcal {K}$, then K∩℘κ∗(M)$\mathcal {K} \cap \wp ^*_\kappa (M)$ is stationary in ℘κ∗(M)$\wp ^*_\kappa (M)$, where ℘κ∗(M)$\wp ^*_\kappa (M)$ denotes the <κ${<}\kappa$‐sized submodules of M$M$ whose intersection with κ$\kappa$ is transitive (i.e., those <κ$<\kappa$‐sized submodules N$N$ of M$M$ such that N∩κ∈κ$N\cap \kappa \in \kappa$).

The set K∩℘κ∗(M)$\mathcal {K}\cap \wp ^*_\kappa (M)$ being stationary in ℘κ∗(M)$\wp ^*_\kappa (M)$ is equivalent to the following statement ([12]): for each function F$F$ from finite subsets of M$M$ into M$M$, there is an X∈K∩℘κ∗(M)$X \in \mathcal {K}\cap \wp ^*_\kappa (M)$ such that X$X$ is closed under the function F$F$. We prove this next.

Fix an arbitrary function F$F$ from finite subsets of M$M$ into M$M$; notice that since F$F$ is finitary, for any infinite D⊂M$D \subset M$, the closure of D$D$ under the function F$F$ has the same cardinality as D$D$. Using the assumption that K$\mathcal {K}$ is ⊆$\subseteq$‐cofinal in [M]<κ$[M]^{<\kappa }$, fix some C0∈K∩[M]<κ$C_0 \in \mathcal {K} \cap [M]^{<\kappa }$. Recursively build a ⊆$\subseteq$‐increasing ω$\omega$‐chain C0⊆X0⊆C1⊆X1⊆C2⊆X2⊆⋯$$\begin{equation*} C_0 \subseteq X_0 \subseteq C_1 \subseteq X_1 \subseteq C_2 \subseteq X_2 \subseteq \dots \end{equation*}$$such that for each n∈ω$n \in \omega$:
Xn$X_n$ is the closure of Cn∪sup(Cn∩κ)$C_n \cup \text{sup}(C_n \cap \kappa)$ under the function F$F$. This closure has cardinality <κ$<\kappa$, because |Cn|<κ$|C_n|<\kappa$ and hence (by regularity of κ$\kappa$) |Cn∪sup(Cn∩κ)|<κ$|C_n \cup \text{sup}(C_n \cap \kappa)| < \kappa$; (for n⩾1$n \geqslant 1$) Cn∈K$C_n \in \mathcal {K}$, Cn⊇Xn−1$C_n \supseteq X_{n-1}$, and |Cn|<κ$|C_n|<\kappa$. This is possible by the assumption that K$\mathcal {K}$ is ⊆$\subseteq$‐cofinal in [M]<κ$[M]^{<\kappa }$ (but note that Cn∩κ$C_n \cap \kappa$ might fail to be transitive). Let X:=⋃n<ωXn$X:= \bigcup _{n<\omega } X_{n}$. Then X$X$ is closed under F$F$, |X|<κ$|X|<\kappa$, and X∩κ=supn<ωsup(Cn∩κ)$X \cap \kappa =\text{sup}_{n < \omega } \text{sup}(C_n \cap \kappa)$; in particular, X∩κ$X \cap \kappa$ is transitive. Also, note that X=⋃n<ωCn$X = \bigcup _{n<\omega } C_n$. Since K$\mathcal {K}$ is closed under quotients, each Cn+1/Cn$C_{n+1}/C_n$ is in K$\mathcal {K}$. So, since K$\mathcal {K}$ is closed under transfinite extensions, and each Cn+1/Cn$C_{n+1}/C_n$ is in K$\mathcal {K}$, we conclude that X∈K$X \in \mathcal {K}$.

Now suppose that K$\mathcal {K}$ is closed under homomorphic images and colimits; we show that (c) implies (b) (and hence (a) will hold too, since closure under homomorphic images trivially implies closure under quotients in the sense of 2). Suppose K$\mathcal {K}$ is bounded in κ$\kappa$. Suppose M∈K$M \in \mathcal {K}$, and fix any X∈[M]<κ$X \in [M]^{<\kappa }$. By κ$\kappa$‐boundedness of K$\mathcal {K}$, for each x∈X$x \in X$ there is a Yx∈K∩[M]<κ$Y_x \in \mathcal {K} \cap [M]^{<\kappa }$ with x∈Yx$x \in Y_x$. Then S:=∑x∈XYx$S:=\sum _{x \in X} Y_x$ is a <κ$<\kappa$‐sized submodule of M$M$ and contains X$X$. And S$S$ is a homomorphic image of the colimit of the (possibly nondirected) diagram of inclusions {Yx→Yz:Yx⊆Yzandx,z∈X}.$$\begin{equation*} \big \lbrace Y_x \rightarrow Y_z \ : \ Y_x \subseteq Y_z \text{ and } x,z \in X \big \rbrace . \end{equation*}$$So, by closure of K$\mathcal {K}$ under homomorphic images and colimits, S∈K$S \in \mathcal {K}$.□$\Box$

section.p:
We now focus on abelian groups. Recall that by Lemma 6 any torsion class ⊥0X${}^{\perp _0} \mathcal {X}$ is closed under homomorphic images, transfinite extensions, and colimits. So by Lemma 11, a class of the form ⊥0X${}^{\perp _0} \mathcal {X}$ is deconstructible if and only if it is bounded in some cardinal. Furthermore, as noted in the introduction, although an ω1$\omega _1$‐strongly compact cardinal might be singular, all cardinals above it are also ω1$\omega _1$‐strongly compact. In particular (by considering its successor if necessary), there exists an ω1$\omega _1$‐strongly compact cardinal if and only if there exists a regular ω1$\omega _1$‐strongly compact cardinal. Then Lemma 6, Lemma 11, and the Corollary 9 of Bagaria and Magidor immediately imply Theorem 2 from the introduction, which asserted that ⊥0Z${}^{\perp _0} \mathbb {Z}$ is deconstructible if and only if there is an ω1$\omega _1$‐strongly compact cardinal. In fact, making use of the Theorem 7 of Bagaria and Magidor, we have:
12 Corollary
The following are equivalent.
(1)There exists an ω1$\omega _1$‐strongly compact cardinal. (2)⊥0Z${}^{\perp _0} \mathbb {Z}$ is deconstructible. (3)For all countable abelian groups X$X$, ⊥0X${}^{\perp _0} X$ is deconstructible.

Since ⊥0Z${}^{\perp _0} \mathbb {Z}$ is closed under transfinite extensions and homomorphic images, we solve part of [6, Question 8.2] in the affirmative:
13 Corollary
Maximum Deconstructibility of [6] has large cardinal consistency strength. Specifically, it lies implication‐wise, in between the existence of an ω1$\omega _1$‐strongly compact and VP.

Recall that deconstructible classes of modules are always precovering ([14, Theorem 7.21]). Thus, another interesting corollary of Corollary 12 and Lemma 6 is the existence of precovering classes (even covering classes) which are not deconstructible:
14 Corollary
If there are no ω1$\omega _1$‐strongly compact cardinals, then there is a covering class in Ab that is closed under colimits, transfinite extensions, and homomorphic images, but is not deconstructible (namely, the class ⊥0Z${}^{\perp _0} \mathbb {Z}$). Thus, ZFC$\mathrm{ZFC}$ cannot prove that all subclasses of Ab satisfying the clauses in Lemma 6 are deconstructible.□$\Box$

mathStatement.title: Remark
mathStatement.p: The following statement has recently been proven in [17, Remark 4 and Corollary 3.4]: Assume VP holds. Then for any ring R$R$, each class of R$R$‐modules that is closed under finite direct sums, extensions, and direct limits is deconstructible.

section.title: QUESTIONS

mathStatement.title: Question
mathStatement.p: Suppose that κ⩾ω2$\kappa \geqslant \omega _2$ is a regular cardinal such that ⊥0X${}^{\perp _0}X$ is deconstructible for all abelian groups of size <κ${<}\kappa$. Must κ$\kappa$ be strongly compact?

section.p: Much of the literature focuses on deconstructibility and precovering properties of “roots of Ext” classes, that is, classes of the form ⊥B:={A:∀B∈BExt1(A,B)=0}$$\begin{equation*} {}^\perp \mathcal {B}:= \big \lbrace A \ : \ \forall B \in \mathcal {B} \ \text{Ext}^1(A,B)=0 \big \rbrace \end{equation*}$$for some fixed class B$\mathcal {B}$ of modules. Our results in Section 5 consistently separates deconstructibility from precovering for ⊥0Z${}^{\perp _0} \mathbb {Z}$, but this is very far from being a root of Ext; it does not even contain the ring Z$\mathbb {Z}$.

This suggests asking whether deconstructibility is equivalent to precovering for classes of the form ⊥B${}^\perp \mathcal {B}$, but there is a caveat: the first author proved in [7] that it is consistent, relative to consistency of VP, that over every hereditary ring (such as Z$\mathbb {Z}$), every class of the form ⊥B${}^\perp \mathcal {B}$ is deconstructible. So, deconstructibility is trivially equivalent to precovering for roots of Ext (over hereditary rings) in that model. But the following questions are open:
17 Question
Is it consistent with ZFC that there is a class B$\mathcal {B}$ of abelian groups such that ⊥B${}^\perp \mathcal {B}$ is precovering, but not deconstructible?

mathStatement.title: Question
mathStatement.p: Does ZFC prove the existence of a ring R$R$ and a class B$\mathcal {B}$ of R$R$‐modules, such that ⊥B${}^\perp \mathcal {B}$ is precovering, but not deconstructible? By the remarks above, such a ring could not be provably hereditary (unless VP is inconsistent).

section.p: Both questions are even open if we replace “classes of the form ⊥B${}^\perp \mathcal {B}$” with “classes that are closed under transfinite extensions and contain the ring” (such classes would contain all free modules).
